Most people judge an Air B N B by one number, the nightly rate. That's the wrong place to start. Here are the five numbers that decide whether a short term rental actually makes money.

Number one, occupancy. That's the share of nights you're actually booked. Sixty two percent means about two hundred twenty six booked nights a year. The other one hundred thirty nine nights earn nothing, but the mortgage still gets paid.

Number two, the nightly rate. Multiply it by your booked nights. A hundred eighty five dollars times two hundred twenty six nights is about forty one thousand eight hundred dollars. Add the cleaning fees guests pay, and gross income here is about forty nine thousand.

Number three, average stay. Short stays mean more turnovers. A three night average is about seventy five guests a year. Every one needs a clean, laundry, and restocking. That's a cost a long term rental barely has.

Number four, the costs people forget. The platform takes a cut. Cleaning costs money. Add utilities, supplies, insurance, property taxes, repairs, and a reserve for big items. In this example, expenses eat about half of the income.

Number five, what's left. Take the income, subtract expenses, and you get net operating income, about twenty five thousand dollars. The mortgage takes twenty one thousand. What remains is cash flow. Three thousand six hundred dollars a year. Divide that by the one hundred eighteen thousand dollars you put in, and cash on cash return is three point oh seven percent.

Now stress test it. Real bookings aren't flat. Drop occupancy from sixty two to fifty two percent, and cash flow flips from three hundred two dollars a month to negative one eighty five. One slow season, and this deal loses money. If a small dip sinks it, the deal is too thin.
